newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Daimler tries to keep Mercedes chief - sources.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Daimler tries to keep Mercedes chief - sources.

text.p: Germany's biggest industrial group Daimler-Benz AG was trying on Monday to persuade Mercedes-Benz chief Helmut Werner to stay on following reports he had threatened to resign, industry sources said.

Following a highly publicised dispute over a planned company reorganisation, Daimler management board chairman Juergen Schrempp had even offered Werner the post of chairman of a restructured Daimler group, the sources said.
Werner has opposed a plan by Schrempp to more closely integrate the profitable Mercedes car and truck operation that has become a cash cow for Daimler.

Werner's contract as management board member of Daimler, which expires at the end of 1997, is up for renewal at a supervisory board meeting on November 6. His contract as head of Mercedes runs until 1999.
But given a possible management revamp, the board may delay a decision to extend the contract, industry sources said, adding that this could prompt Werner to resign.
"Everybody wants to keep Werner in the company," one source said.

The deputy chairman of the supervisory board, Karl Feuerstein said in an interview that any supervisory board decision on a restructuring of Daimler would probably not be taken at the November 6 meeting.
"Maybe the decision won't be taken this year," said Feuerstein, who is also chairman of the group's works council.
Feuerstein said he was not opposed to the idea of a new structure but believed Daimler's automotive business must remain a single entity.
"We will measure all proposals according to this demand," he said.

The four-member executive committee of the supervisory board, consisting of two employee and two shareholder representatives, will discuss the plans for a management restructuring at a meeting on Tuesday, Feuerstein said.

Sources close to the company said shareholder representatives on the supervisory board, including Deutsche Bank chief executive Hilmar Kopper, would meet on Monday to discuss the changes. Deutsche owns 24.3 percent of Daimler.

Feuerstein also attacked what he called deliberate "indiscretions" coming from Daimler's head office which resulted in weekend newspaper reports that Schrempp had persuaded three Mercedes managers to agree to his merger plan.

The plan to integrate Mercedes with its parent company is seen as part of a drive by Schrempp to take Daimler back to its roots as a transport group, reversing the trend begun by his predecessor Edzard Reuter to create an integrated technology holding group.

Analysts have said the plan would be a logical next step following the dissolution earlier this year of Daimler's loss-making AEG industrial division and the divestment of the majority-held Fokker planemaker in the Netherlands.

Mercedes, which now makes up around three-quarters of Daimler's group revenues, has predicted its 1996 profits will be "clearly" higher than last year's 2.275 billion mark ($1.48 billion) profit, the Boersen-Zeitung reported on Saturday. --Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
